paras: The intimidation of Charles Jackson at Boeuf River was a threat made in January 1903 against Jackson, a Black mail carrier in Louisiana, by white men who ordered him not to return with the mail on his route and threatened him with death if he did. The Post Office Department sent an inspector to investigate, but no report of his findings or of any arrest appears in the coverage. The threat drew national notice because it coincided with the closing of the Indianola, Mississippi, post office, and papers treated it as part of a Southern campaign against Black federal employees.

Jackson was described in the wire report as "a negro mail carrier" and by the Cleveland Gazette as "the rural delivery carrier" serving Boeuf River. The report reached Washington while Postmaster General Payne was dealing with Indianola, where the post office had been closed "as a result of antagonism to the negro postmaster," Minnie Cox.

According to a Washington dispatch dated January 5, Payne received information that day that "a posse of white citizens" at Boeuf River had, "last night," ordered Jackson not to return with the mail on his route and threatened him with death. The Washington Evening Star and the Shreveport Caucasian placed the threat on "Sunday night," which also points to January 4. The reason the men gave, in the dispatch's words, was "the color of the carrier"; the Evening Star called it "race prejudice" and wrote that Jackson's "life would pay the forfeit" if he returned.
None of the men was named or counted, and the New-York Tribune's version of the dispatch called them "a mob of white men" rather than a posse.

The case was reported to the postal authorities, and Post Office Inspector Peters of the New Orleans division was dispatched to Girard with orders to make "a thorough investigation." On January 6 the Evening Star reported that Peters had been notified by telegraph and had "hurried to the scene," but that no report had yet been received from him. Later, the Cleveland Gazette added that so far as the department knew Jackson bore "a good character," and that it would "settle with" the men. No report of the inspector's findings, of arrests, or of whether Jackson resumed his route was found.

White papers ran the Washington dispatch on January 6 with little change, from the Richmond Dispatch, Savannah Morning News and Montgomery Advertiser to the Louisville Courier-Journal and the San Francisco Call. Their headlines differed in emphasis: the Indianapolis Journal's read "Bulldozed by Whites," the Savannah paper's "Whites Threatened Negro Mail Carrier," and the San Francisco Call's "Posse of Louisiana Whites Interferes With Federal Employe." The Montgomery Advertiser's subhead hedged that the "Negro Employee of Government" was "Said to Have Been Ordered to Leave." In Louisiana, the only paper found carrying it, the Shreveport Caucasian, printed the wire text under "Threats Made" without comment.

Northern white editorials folded the case into the Indianola controversy: the Indianapolis Journal's "The New Rebellion" cited the threat by "a mob of white men" as further evidence of resistance to Black federal officeholders. A Chicago Evening Post editorial reprinted in the Worthington Advance listed the warning that the carrier "will be killed" among signs of the "lawless mob element of the South."

The Black weeklies took up the story a few days later, the Iowa State Bystander reprinting the wire text under "Colored Mail Carrier Threatened" and the Indianapolis Freeman running it beside the Indianola news under "Postoffice Troubles." The St. Paul Appeal mentioned the carrier ordered off his route "under penalty of being killed" in an editorial defending President Roosevelt's handling of Indianola. The Cleveland Gazette went furthest, opening its item by declaring that "the crusade in Louisiana against Afro-American postal employees has commenced" and calling the men "white brutes" and "cowardly brutes."

The reports differ on the date: the January 5 dispatch said "last night" and the Evening Star "Sunday night," while a one-line digest in the Grenada Sentinel dated the threat "on the 5th." The dispatch and the Star are the earlier, fuller sources; the Sentinel may have dated the event by the day the news reached Washington.

reader.title: Intimidation of Charles Jackson at Boeuf River
bases: A group of white men ordered a Black federal mail carrier off his route on threat of death; no one was harmed, and the order was to stop carrying the mail rather than to leave the community (A1, A4, A25).

Every account traces to the one report the Post Office Department received on Jan. 5, relayed by wire (A1, A2) and in the Evening Star's own Washington item (A4); no local Louisiana report, inspector's report or other independent account was found (A17).

framing.detail: Most papers, North and South, ran the Jan. 5 dispatch unchanged under headlines such as 'Whites Threatened Negro Mail Carrier' and 'Negro Mail Carrier Threatened by Whites'.
The Indianapolis Journal headlined it 'Bulldozed by Whites' and its editorial 'The New Rebellion' cited it as evidence of resistance to Black federal officeholders.
A Chicago Evening Post editorial reprinted in the Worthington Advance listed the threat among acts of the 'lawless mob element of the South'.
The Montgomery Advertiser's subhead hedged that the employee was 'Said to Have Been Ordered to Leave'; the Shreveport Caucasian ran the wire text as 'Threats Made' with no comment.
The Iowa State Bystander and Indianapolis Freeman reprinted the wire text, the Freeman beside the Indianola news under 'Postoffice Troubles'.

The Cleveland Gazette called the men 'white brutes' and 'cowardly brutes' and the case the start of a Louisiana 'crusade' against Afro-American postal employees; the St. Paul Appeal folded it into an editorial attacking Southern resistance at Indianola.
